extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, history of science, and readers studying Bacon's Novum Organum and methods of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Bacon's rules for collecting instances, constructing Tables, and performing induction (Methods of Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues, and Rejections), plus practical experimental guidance for detecting subtle phenomena (e.g., heat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Tables (ministratio ad memoriam)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ministratio ad memoriam' arranges collected instances in Tables, in a form adapted for use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables in the Novum Organum are specimens of what Bacon designed; the order of arrangement must be determined after collection, according to the actual order in which instances present themselves to the investigator (not any predetermined order), so as to avoid overlooking materially relevant instances. The Tables are preparatory to induction and to the subsequent 'ministratio ad mentem' (drawing inferences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process of Induction (ministratio ad mentem sive rationem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ministratio ad mentem sive rationem' is the process of Induction itself, drawing from the Tables the inferences to which they legitimately lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tables serve as the factual basis from which induction is to be performed; construction of Tables and application of methods (agreement, difference, concomitant variations, rejections) are part of a single process leading to inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of arrangement — empirical ordering, not predetermined
rubrics_metrics.description: Order instances according to the actual order they present themselves to the investigator, not according to any predetermined order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the order after collection when all instances are before us, otherwise there is danger of overlooking instances material to enquiry. The arrangement should reflect empirical observation rather than a preconceived scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the 'Instantiae convenientes' are so related that, besides the given phenomenon, only one other circumstance is common to them all, that other circumstance may be regarded (with probability) as the cause (or effect) or connected with it by causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a Table of Agreement consisting of instances that all present the phenomenon and share only one other circumstance; that common circumstance is a candidate cause/effect. Use as part of the suite of methods — not necessarily decisive alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: When one instance in the Table of Agreement is matched with one in the Table of Privation that share every circumstance except (a) the presence/absence of the phenomenon and (b) one other circumstance, that other circumstance is the cause (or effect) or a necessary part of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value of such paired instances depends on their approximation in other respects — the closer they agree aside from the differing circumstance, the more likely one can detect the cause. Use negative instances that are 'in proximo' (closely akin) to the positive ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: If in the 'Tabula graduum' some phenomenon increases and diminishes proportionately with the increase and diminution of the given phenomenon (e.g., heat), that concurrent variation identifies a cause or effect, or connection by causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If that phenomenon and the given phenomenon are the only circumstances varying concurrently, then it can be proved to be either cause or effect. The method looks for proportional covariation across instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabula of Privations / Negative Instances (declinationis / absentiae in proximo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negatives (privations) are to be inspected only in subjects most closely related to those in which the nature is present; the 'Tabulam declinationis' or 'absentiae in proximo' collects instances in which the given nature is absent in closely akin subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because forms/causes must also be absent where the given nature is absent, negative instances should be chosen among those 'maxime cognata' to the positives so as to reduce the search space and avoid infinite lists of unrelated negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplum exclusivae / Method of Rejections (Exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections consist in excluding some possible explanation of the phenomenon because (a) an instance which does not present the phenomenon does present the assigned cause, or (b) an instance which does present the phenomenon does not present the assigned cause (and similarly with increase and decrease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A succession of these 'rejectiones' limits the number of possible explanations among which to seek the true one. Bacon's rejections are typically not exhaustive and so often lead only to negative results — they can save trouble but, unlike the Method of Residues, may not leave a definite finite set of antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues (relation to Bacon's rejectiones)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Exemplum exclusivae' bears some resemblance to the Method of Residues, but Bacon's rejections are not truly exhaustive and therefore usually yield only a negative result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of Residues aims to leave a definite number of antecedents which either constitute the cause or among which the cause must be sought; Bacon's approach via rejections does not always achieve that exhaustiveness and thus is weaker in producing certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for Perfect Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: If there were a certain finite number only of possible causes, and by the Method of Rejections we could exclude all but one, the remaining one would be the undoubted cause — the perfect type of Induction capable of affording certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon regarded this singular remaining-cause situation as the ideal and sole means of achieving logical certainty by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent use of Tables and Methods (Baconian procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon contemplated the concurrent use of all the Tables (Agreement, Difference, Degrees, Privations) as preparatory to his Method of Rejections; construction of Tables and subsequent application of Rejections constitute one process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Mill: Mill's methods may be worked independently to final conclusion; Bacon treated the tables as jointly preparatory, to be used together in a single inductive enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Approximation of Instances for Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: The significance of paired instances (e.g., one positive and one negative) depends on the extent of their approximation in other respects; the more closely they approach in all other respects, the more likely we are to detect the cause of variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select instances that are similar in as many respects as possible except the critical differing circumstance; emphasis on 'approximation' reduces confounding differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental protocol guidance for detecting subtle phenomena (heat in lunar rays etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical experiments are suggested: use well-fabricated burning mirrors (specula comburentia), lenses (vitrum), and 'vitrum calcidare' to collect/refocus rays; interpose mirrors between hand and sunlight to observe increase/decrease of heat; collect lunar rays with burning mirrors and test for slightest degree of warmth using sensitive glass or depression of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the degree of heat is too subtle to be perceived by touch, resort to instruments (glass indicating constitution of air, thermometers, focused mirrors/lenses). Perform experiments comparing reflected vs direct rays, use mirrors in common flame, test heating of non-luminous heated bodies (iron, heated stone), and observe boiling/depression of water as measurable effects. Examples: Melloni, Saussure, Pictet experiments later confirmed heat-radiation; use of concave mirrors to increase heat at focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate instruments when sensations are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: When a grade of the phenomenon is too subtle to be perceived by touch (or other direct senses), one must use instruments (e.g., glass indicators, thermometers, lenses and mirrors) to detect and measure it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confess the limitations of unaided senses; employ the best available apparatus (glass to show air constitution, thermometers, burning mirrors, lenses) and note measurable changes (depression of water, heating of iron/stone, boiling) rather than relying solely on subjective sensation.
